buildUp: Start with the science: infrared light from very faint, distant objects, which needs a big mirror, and a cold telescope so its own glow doesn't drown the signal.

On Earth the warm atmosphere glows and absorbs infrared, so the telescope goes to space, to a spot about 1.5 million km away where the Sun, Earth and Moon always lie in roughly the same direction and one shield can block them all.

A shield facing the Sun lets the telescope cool by radiating into dark space, and five thin, separated layers block heat far better than one thick one; the warm spacecraft with its solar array, computers and radio sits on the sunny side.
A 6.5 m mirror won't fit in any rocket, so it is split into 18 light beryllium hexagons on a folding backplane, coated in gold because gold reflects infrared superbly.

Folded segments can't be placed perfectly, so each has tiny actuators to move it in steps of roughly 10 nanometres, and the secondary mirror on its struts can be adjusted too, until all of them focus as one.

Finally, light passes through the aft optics into a box of cameras and spectrographs behind the mirror, one of which needs an extra cooler to reach about 7 K, while star trackers and a fine guidance sensor hold the view steady.
firstPrinciples.coreIdea: Put a huge, foldable mirror in permanent shade. A sunshield the size of a tennis court always faces the Sun, Earth and Moon, so the telescope behind it cools itself by radiating its heat into the darkness of space. The mirror is made of 18 segments that fold up for launch and are then adjusted with tiny motors until they act as one smooth surface.

hardParts.title: Unfolding a tennis court with no second chance
hardParts.why: The sunshield's five layers, each thinner than a hair, had to be folded into a rocket, then unrolled and pulled taut by booms, cables and pulleys with around 140 release mechanisms, any one of which could have jammed. Nothing so big and so delicate can be fully tested on Earth, where gravity and air behave nothing like space, and no one could go out to fix it.

hardParts.title: Making 18 mirrors behave as one
hardParts.why: For a sharp image the segments must line up to within a few tens of nanometres, thousands of times thinner than a hair, after a violent launch and cooling by hundreds of degrees. Engineers worked from images of a single star, nudging each segment's actuators until 18 separate star images merged into one, and the backplane has to hold that alignment for months without bending.

hardParts.title: Getting cold enough, and staying still
hardParts.why: Most of the telescope cools itself in the shade, but the longest-wavelength instrument needs a mechanical cooler to reach about 7 K without shaking the optics. Materials shrink as they cool, so everything had to be designed to end up in exactly the right shape at its frozen working temperature, not the warm one it was built at.

principles.explanation: Anything near room temperature glows in exactly the infrared this telescope looks for, so it must be kept very cold or its own glow would drown out the stars. Every object gives off light because of its temperature, and the colder it is, the longer the wavelength where that glow peaks. A rough rule is that the peak wavelength in micrometres is about 2,900 divided by the temperature in kelvin: the Sun at about 5,800 K peaks in visible light, while a room-temperature object at about 300 K peaks around 10 micrometres, right in the middle of this telescope's range. A warm telescope would be like trying to see stars with a torch shining in your eye. Cooling it to around 40 K moves its own glow out to far longer wavelengths, clear of the light it is looking for.
principles.title: Everything warm glows in infrared

principles.explanation: The expanding universe has stretched the light of the first galaxies into infrared, so to see them at all a telescope has to look in infrared. As space expands, light travelling through it is stretched along with it, so its wavelength grows; this is called redshift. Light that left the first galaxies as ultraviolet and visible light has been travelling for over 13 billion years, and has been stretched so much that it arrives as infrared. Infrared also slips through dust that blocks visible light, which is why it reveals stars forming inside dark clouds.
principles.title: The expanding universe stretches light

principles.explanation: A wider mirror catches more of the scarce photons and makes sharper images, and infrared's long waves make width matter even more, which is why this one is 6.5 m across. A mirror is a bucket for light: its collecting area, roughly 25 square metres here, sets how many of the few incoming photons you catch, and so how faint you can see. It also sets sharpness, because waves passing through an opening spread out, by an angle of roughly the wavelength divided by the mirror's width. Infrared waves are longer than visible ones, so an infrared telescope needs an even wider mirror to see the same fine detail. At 2 micrometres a 6.5 m mirror can separate points less than a tenth of an arcsecond apart, roughly the size of a coin seen from tens of kilometres away.
principles.title: Bigger mirrors gather more and see finer

principles.explanation: In the vacuum of space heat can only cross a gap by radiating, so a stack of separated shiny layers can keep almost all of the Sun's heat off the telescope. On Earth, heat leaks away through air and anything touching it, but in space the only way heat moves between separate surfaces is by glowing. A shiny, metal-coated layer reflects most of the sunlight that hits it and gives off little of its own heat. Stack five such layers with gaps between them, angled so the gaps open towards the edges, and each layer passes only a fraction of the heat to the next while the rest radiates sideways into space. Sunlight brings roughly 1.4 kilowatts onto every square metre facing the Sun, yet only a tiny trickle reaches the telescope side.
principles.title: In space, heat only travels as radiation

firstPrinciples.problem: See the faintest, most distant things in the universe, the first galaxies and stars being born inside dust clouds, whose light arrives mostly as infrared, a few photons at a time. Infrared is heat, so the telescope itself, the Earth, the Sun and even the instruments all glow brightly in exactly the light you're trying to catch. You need a mirror bigger than any rocket can carry, kept colder than -220 °C and stiller than a few billionths of a metre, a million and a half kilometres from anyone who could fix it.

questions.answer: Gold reflects infrared light extremely well, a little better than aluminium, though it reflects blue light poorly. For an infrared telescope that trade is worth it, and only a very thin layer is needed.
questions.question: Why is the mirror coated in gold rather than the aluminium used on most telescopes?

questions.answer: In space, heat crosses gaps only by radiating. Each separated layer reflects most of what reaches it and lets the heat between layers escape sideways, so the heat reaching the telescope drops sharply with every layer, much more than a single solid sheet would manage.
questions.question: Why use five thin layers in the sunshield instead of one thick, heavy one?

questions.answer: Near Earth, the Sun and the warm Earth would be in very different directions and keep moving around the sky, so no single shield could keep both off the telescope. Far away, all three stay on one side, and one shield can block them all at once.
questions.question: Why couldn't this telescope just orbit close to Earth like many others?

firstPrinciples.xFactor: The real trick is that the telescope is cooled almost entirely for free: no fridge, just a shield and the cold of deep space. By choosing an orbit where the Sun, Earth and Moon always sit on one side, a few hair-thin sheets of coated plastic can hold a 6.5 m mirror around 300 °C colder than the side facing the Sun, which is what makes seeing the faint glow of the first galaxies possible at all.

name: Space Telescope
overview:
This telescope sees the universe in infrared light, which lets it look through dust clouds at stars being born and catch the stretched, reddened light of the very first galaxies. To do that it has to be extraordinarily cold, because anything warm glows in infrared and would drown out the faint signals. So the telescope sits on top of a huge sunshield that always faces the Sun, Earth and Moon, keeping the mirror and instruments in permanent shadow.

The main mirror is 6.5 m across, far too big to launch in one piece, so it's made of 18 hexagonal segments of beryllium coated in a thin layer of gold, which reflects infrared light superbly. It launched folded up like origami and unfolded in space; tiny motors behind every segment then nudged them into alignment to within a fraction of the width of a hair.

Light bounces off the big mirror to a small secondary mirror held out on struts, back down through the centre, and into a box of cameras and spectrographs behind the mirror. Below the sunshield, on the warm side, the spacecraft bus carries the solar panel, computers, fuel and the radio that sends the pictures home from 1.5 million kilometres away.

parts.description: Six gold-coated beryllium hexagons in the inner ring of the main mirror.

details.didYouKnow: On the James Webb Space Telescope the segments come in three slightly different curved shapes, labelled A, B and C, six of each; the six inner-ring segments are the A segments. Their surface was shaped so it would only become exactly right once it had cooled down in space.
details.howItWorks: Together with the other 12 segments, these form one huge curved mirror that gathers faint infrared light and focuses it onto the secondary mirror. On their own the 18 hexagons would make 18 separate, blurry images, so after launch engineers spent months nudging each one until all 18 worked as a single smooth surface. The inner ring sits closest to the central hole, through which the light is bounced back down to the aft optics.
keyNumbers: About 1.32 m across, flat to flat
Roughly 20 kg of beryllium per mirror
Gold coating only about 100 nanometres thick
18 segments share roughly 48 g of gold in total
details.madeOf: Each segment is a polished beryllium blank, mostly hollowed out at the back into a ribbed honeycomb, with a microscopically thin layer of gold on the front. Beryllium is light and stiff and barely changes shape at the extreme cold the telescope works at, and gold reflects infrared light extremely well.

parts.name: Inner mirror segments

parts.description: Six segments filling the flat sides of the outer ring; each can be tilted and bent by tiny motors.

details.didYouKnow: In early 2022 Webb's first test image of a star showed 18 separate dots, one from each segment, which were then slowly stacked into one sharp point. In May 2022 a dust-sized micrometeoroid struck one of the outer segments, and engineers partly corrected the damage by readjusting it.
details.howItWorks: Behind each segment are seven actuators: six arranged to shift and tilt it, and one in the middle that pushes or pulls to change how strongly it curves. Working from test images of a bright star, engineers adjust them in steps far smaller than a bacterium until the light from every segment lands in exactly the same place. The adjustments are rare once aligned, because the cold, stable telescope barely drifts.
keyNumbers: 7 actuators per segment
Actuator steps of roughly 10 nanometres
About 132 actuators across all the mirrors
Fine alignment finished in March 2022
details.madeOf: Gold-coated beryllium, like the other segments, mounted on a small support frame that connects the actuators to the backplane. The actuators themselves are motor-driven mechanisms built to work at temperatures colder than -220 °C.

parts.name: Outer mirror segments (sides)

parts.description: Six segments at the corners of the outer ring, giving the mirror its 6.5 m span.

details.didYouKnow: The two mirror wings unfolded on 7 and 8 January 2022, completing Webb's major deployments about two weeks after launch.
details.howItWorks: The corner segments set the overall width of the mirror, and the wider a mirror is, the finer the detail it can see. The mirror was too big to fit inside the rocket, so the outer edges were mounted on two side wings that folded back like the leaves of a drop-leaf table for launch. Once in space the wings swung forward and latched, and the segments on them were then aligned with the rest.
keyNumbers: Mirror about 6.5 m from corner to corner
Collecting area roughly 25 square metres
About 6 times the light-collecting area of Hubble
details.madeOf: Gold-coated beryllium, the same as their neighbours. Polishing was done in rounds: each segment was chilled to working temperature, measured, warmed up, and polished again to correct the tiny distortions the cold caused.

parts.name: Outer mirror segments (corners)

parts.description: Small round convex mirror held out in front of the main mirror, bouncing the light back down through the centre.

details.didYouKnow: The secondary mirror swung out into position on 5 January 2022, one of the most nervously watched moments of the deployment.
details.howItWorks: Light reflected by the big primary mirror converges on this small mirror, which bounces it back towards the hole in the middle of the primary. It is gently domed outwards, which stretches the effective focal length of the telescope so the image is large enough for the instruments. It has its own six actuators so it can be shifted and tilted to line up with the 18 segments.
keyNumbers: About 0.74 m across
Held roughly 7 to 8 m in front of the primary mirror
6 actuators to adjust its position
details.madeOf: Gold-coated beryllium, for the same reasons as the main mirror: light, stiff and steady when cold, with a coating that reflects infrared superbly.

parts.name: Secondary mirror

parts.description: Three long, light carbon-composite struts that unfolded in space to hold the secondary mirror precisely in place.

details.didYouKnow: Bright stars in Webb pictures show six large spikes from the hexagonal mirror edges, plus two smaller horizontal ones caused by the vertical strut.
details.howItWorks: The three struts form a tripod that holds the secondary mirror out in front of the primary, and they have to keep it in place to within a tiny fraction of a millimetre. For launch they lay folded against the mirror; in space, motors swung them out and latched them. They are thin to block as little incoming light as possible, and their shadows are what create some of the spikes seen around bright stars in Webb images.
keyNumbers: About 8 m long
3 struts in a tripod
Working below about -220 °C
details.madeOf: Long tubes of carbon-fibre composite, which is very stiff for its weight and expands very little as temperatures change.

parts.name: Secondary mirror struts

parts.description: Tower in the centre of the main mirror holding the tertiary and steering mirrors that feed light to the instruments.

details.didYouKnow: Unlike the secondary mirror and the mirror wings, the aft optics did not need to unfold; the tower sits fixed at the centre of the primary mirror throughout.
details.howItWorks: Light from the secondary mirror comes down through the hole in the primary into this tower, which contains the tertiary mirror and the fine steering mirror. The tertiary mirror corrects the image and passes it on, and the fine steering mirror makes tiny, rapid tilts to cancel any wobble, using measurements from the guidance sensor. Its baffled shape also blocks stray light from reaching the instruments directly.
keyNumbers: Contains 2 mirrors, tertiary and fine steering
Steering corrections many times per second
Image held steady to within a few thousandths of an arcsecond
details.madeOf: A carbon-composite and metal structure holding small beryllium mirrors. Everything has to stay stable at deep-space temperatures so the light path does not drift.

parts.name: Aft optics

parts.description: Stiff carbon-composite frame behind the mirror segments that holds them steady to within billionths of a metre.

details.didYouKnow: The backplane was tested in huge cold chambers on Earth, because a structure that seems perfectly stiff at room temperature can warp slightly when chilled to deep-space temperatures.
details.howItWorks: The backplane is the skeleton the whole telescope hangs from: it carries the 18 mirror segments, the secondary mirror struts and the instrument module beneath. Like the mirror, it is built in three sections so the two side wings could fold back for launch and lock rigidly in place in space. Its job is to stay so still that the segments keep their alignment for weeks or months without correction.
keyNumbers: Supports a mirror about 6.5 m across
Held stable to within roughly tens of nanometres
Operates below about 50 K (around -223 °C)
details.madeOf: Graphite composite tubes and panels, joined with titanium and invar fittings. These materials were chosen because they barely expand or shrink as temperatures change, and the composite is light enough to launch.

parts.name: Mirror backplane

parts.description: Box behind the mirror holding the infrared cameras, spectrographs and guidance sensor.

details.didYouKnow: NIRSpec contains a grid of about a quarter of a million tiny shutters, each roughly the width of a few human hairs, that open to let in light from chosen galaxies and close to block everything else.
details.howItWorks: The Integrated Science Instrument Module holds the four science instruments that turn collected light into data: NIRCam, NIRSpec, MIRI and FGS/NIRISS. NIRCam takes images, NIRSpec splits light into spectra to reveal what distant objects are made of, MIRI covers longer mid-infrared wavelengths, and the Fine Guidance Sensor locks onto guide stars to keep the telescope pointed. Most of the instruments are cooled passively by the sunshield, but MIRI needs a cryocooler to get even colder.
keyNumbers: 4 science instruments
Covers roughly 0.6 to 28 micrometres in wavelength
MIRI cooled to about 7 K (-266 °C)
NIRSpec can study up to about 100 objects at once
details.madeOf: A frame of carbon composite holding the instruments, wrapped in thermal blankets. The instruments contain mirrors, filters, gratings and infrared detectors, mostly made from special semiconductors such as mercury cadmium telluride.

parts.name: Science instruments

parts.description: Telescoping column that extended in space to lift the telescope away from the warm spacecraft below.

details.didYouKnow: Webb's deployment sequence involved hundreds of single-use release mechanisms that all had to work in the right order, with no way to send anyone out to fix one.
details.howItWorks: The tower connects the telescope to the spacecraft bus, and once in space it extended to push them apart. The extra distance lets the cold telescope sit well away from the warm electronics, and leaves room for the sunshield to spread between them. It also helps keep vibrations from the spacecraft's spinning reaction wheels away from the delicate optics.
keyNumbers: Extended about 1.2 m
Extended in space on 31 December 2021
Links a near room-temperature bus to optics below about -220 °C
details.madeOf: Telescoping tubes with metal and composite parts, driven by a motor. It has to be strong enough to carry launch loads but stiff once extended.

parts.name: Deployable tower

parts.description: Top layer, nearest the telescope and the coldest, at well under -200 °C.

details.didYouKnow: The full sunshield gives the telescope protection often described as like sunscreen with an SPF of about one million.
details.howItWorks: This top layer is the last barrier before the telescope, and by the time heat has fought its way up through the four layers below, very little is left. It faces the cold optics, so it is one of the coldest large surfaces on the observatory. Like the others, it is pulled taut by cables so it stays flat and evenly spaced from its neighbours.
keyNumbers: About 0.025 mm thick
Down to roughly -237 °C
Shield roughly 21 x 14 m overall
details.madeOf: Kapton E plastic film coated with a thin layer of aluminium. On the James Webb Space Telescope this layer is one of the thinnest of the five.

parts.name: Sunshield layer 1 (top, coldest)

parts.description: Second layer; each gap between layers lets heat radiate out sideways into space.

details.didYouKnow: Engineers compare the layered design to a stack of mirrors with gaps between, rather than a blanket; a blanket would just conduct heat straight through.
details.howItWorks: Each layer only lets a fraction of the heat through to the next, mostly as infrared glow. The layers are held apart, and the gaps between them widen towards the edges, so heat radiating between them escapes sideways out into space rather than continuing upwards. That is why five separated thin layers work much better than one thick one.
keyNumbers: About 0.025 mm thick
Gaps between layers widen towards the edges
Sits second from the telescope side
details.madeOf: Aluminium-coated Kapton E film. The aluminium is shiny to infrared, so each layer reflects most of the heat reaching it.

parts.name: Sunshield layer 2 (second)

parts.description: Middle layer of the five, a sheet of plastic film thinner than a human hair.

details.didYouKnow: The rip-stop seams were added because a film this thin can be torn by a sharp edge, and during ground testing the sunshield did suffer tears that had to be repaired.
details.howItWorks: The middle layer sits roughly halfway down the temperature drop between the hot sunward side and the cold telescope side. Each layer is a slightly different size and shape so the stack forms the right wedge-shaped spacing. Woven into it is a grid of reinforced seams that stops any small tear from spreading.
keyNumbers: About 0.025 mm thick
Each layer roughly the size of a tennis court
Middle of 5 layers
details.madeOf: Aluminium-coated Kapton E, a polyimide film that stays flexible and stable over a very wide range of temperatures.

parts.name: Sunshield layer 3 (middle)

parts.description: Fourth layer; like the others it's coated in aluminium to reflect heat away.

details.didYouKnow: The doped silicon coating is slightly conductive, which helps bleed away electric charge that would otherwise build up on the shield in space.
details.howItWorks: As one of the two layers nearest the Sun, this one does heavy work rejecting heat before it can travel further up the stack. It receives heat radiated from the hot bottom layer and sends most of it out sideways. Its coating also needs to stand up to the strong sunlight and charged particles reaching that side.
keyNumbers: About 0.025 mm thick
Silicon coating roughly 50 nanometres thick
Fourth of 5 layers from the telescope
details.madeOf: Kapton E with aluminium, and an extra coating of doped silicon on its sun-facing side. The silicon helps reflect sunlight and carry away heat, and gives this side of the shield a purplish tint.

parts.name: Sunshield layer 4 (fourth)

parts.description: Bottom layer facing the Sun, the hottest at over 80 °C, coated to bounce sunlight away.

details.didYouKnow: Webb's numbering goes the other way round: NASA calls this sunward film Layer 1 and the one nearest the telescope Layer 5.
details.howItWorks: This bottom layer takes the full force of the Sun and bounces away most of the light and heat that hits it. Because the observatory always keeps its shield facing the Sun, this layer always stays hot while the top of the stack stays bitterly cold. The temperature difference across just five films is hundreds of degrees.
keyNumbers: About 0.05 mm thick, twice the others
Up to about 110 °C on the hot side
Total drop of roughly 300 °C to the cold side
details.madeOf: Kapton E film coated with aluminium and doped silicon. It is the thickest layer, giving it extra toughness for the side most exposed to sunlight and tiny meteoroids.

parts.name: Sunshield layer 5 (bottom, sunward)

parts.description: Telescoping booms that slid out sideways in space to pull the folded sunshield layers taut.

details.didYouKnow: The sunshield's deployment was considered the most complex part of the whole sequence, and it played out over about a week of carefully checked steps commanded from the ground.
details.howItWorks: The two mid-booms extend sideways from the centre of the observatory, unrolling the folded layers outwards as they go. Once all the booms are out, motors pull a network of cables to tension each layer and separate it from its neighbours. Front and back pallets carried the folded shield and unfolded it from fore to aft before the booms widened it.
keyNumbers: Shield about 21 m wide once out
About 140 release mechanisms on the sunshield
Roughly 400 pulleys and 90 cables
Fully tensioned on 4 January 2022
details.madeOf: Telescoping carbon-composite tubes, light enough to launch and stiff enough to hold the huge shield steady. The cables run over pulleys and are driven by motors.

parts.name: Sunshield booms

parts.description: Body of the spacecraft on the warm side of the shield, with the computers, fuel, thrusters and pointing gear.

details.didYouKnow: Webb's Ariane 5 launch on 25 December 2021 was so accurate that the mission saved fuel on its course corrections, which is why it should last well beyond its 10-year goal.
details.howItWorks: The bus is the support system for the telescope: it supplies power, runs the flight computers, stores and sends data, and steers the observatory. Reaction wheels spin up or slow down to turn it without using fuel, while small thrusters handle orbit corrections and unload built-up momentum caused by sunlight pushing on the sunshield. It sits on the warm, Sun-facing side, so its electronics run near room temperature.
keyNumbers: About 68 GB solid-state recorder
Orbits around L2, about 1.5 million km from Earth
Fuel expected to last roughly 20 years
details.madeOf: A graphite composite structure holding electronics boxes, propellant tanks, thrusters and wiring, wrapped in thermal blankets.

parts.name: Spacecraft bus

parts.description: Single fold-out panel of solar cells that always faces the Sun and powers the whole observatory.

details.didYouKnow: The array unfolded automatically just minutes after Webb separated from its rocket, slightly earlier than planned, which was the first deployment of the mission.
details.howItWorks: The array turns sunlight into electricity for everything on board, from the instruments and cryocooler to the radios and heaters. It extends from the bus on the Sun-facing side and its panels deploy in a line from a folded stack. Because the shield must always face the Sun, the array stays in sunlight at L2 with no nights to interrupt it.
keyNumbers: About 2 kW of power
Deployed about half an hour after launch
Always in sunlight at L2
details.madeOf: Solar cells mounted on light, rigid panels. Space-grade cells are typically made from layered semiconductors that turn more of the sunlight into power than household panels.

parts.name: Solar array

parts.description: Steerable dish under the spacecraft that beams the science data back to the big radio dishes on Earth.

details.didYouKnow: Webb records data on board and dumps it to Earth during scheduled contacts each day, rather than streaming everything as it observes.
details.howItWorks: The high-gain antenna points at Earth and sends down science images and spectra to NASA's Deep Space Network dishes in California, Spain and Australia. It is steerable so it can stay locked on Earth as the observatory turns to look at different targets. Commands and housekeeping data use a slower S-band link, while the bulk of the science comes down on the faster Ka-band.
keyNumbers: Ka-band data at up to about 28 Mbit/s
Roughly 57 GB of science data per day at most
Sends across about 1.5 million km
details.madeOf: A lightweight dish and feed on a motorised mount, built to withstand the cold and the launch vibration.

parts.name: High-gain antenna

parts.description: Pair of small cameras that recognise star patterns to tell the spacecraft exactly which way it's pointing.

details.didYouKnow: Webb cannot point anywhere near the Sun, so at any one time it can only observe a band of the sky; over a year, as it orbits the Sun, it can see the whole sky.
details.howItWorks: Each star tracker is a small camera that photographs a patch of sky and compares the pattern of stars with an onboard catalogue to work out exactly which way the observatory is facing. This tells the computers how to fire the reaction wheels when slewing to a new target. Once on target, the Fine Guidance Sensor in the telescope takes over for the extremely precise pointing.
keyNumbers: 2 trackers for backup
Attitude updated several times per second
Mounted on the warm, Sun-facing spacecraft bus
details.madeOf: A lens and light sensor in a housing with a long shade to block stray light from the Sun and the spacecraft, plus electronics to recognise star patterns.

parts.name: Star trackers

parts.description: Stiff bars at the tips of the booms that hold the five films apart, so the gaps stay open where heat escapes.

details.didYouKnow: The separation matters so much that the shield's shape was tuned so that each gap opens wider towards the edge, which is one reason it looks like a kite rather than a flat sheet.
details.howItWorks: If two films touched, heat would conduct straight across and the shield would lose much of its power. The bars at the boom tips hold each layer's corner at a set height, opening the stack out like the pages of a fanned book. The wider gaps at the edges give the heat trapped between layers a clear path out into space.
keyNumbers: 5 cleats, one for each layer
Gaps open to a few tens of centimetres at the tips
One bar at each end of the long booms
details.madeOf: Light, stiff composite tubes with small metal cleats and pulleys for the tensioning cables. They have to stay straight across a large temperature difference from one end to the other.

parts.name: Spreader bars

parts.description: Fold-down platforms at the front and back that carried the folded sunshield through launch, then swung out to start unfolding it.

details.didYouKnow: Getting the shield out took several days, and every step had to be commanded from the ground in turn, so engineers could stop and check before moving on.
details.howItWorks: For launch the whole sunshield was folded up like an accordion and strapped onto these two platforms, packing a tennis-court-sized sheet around the telescope. In space, motors swung them down to their open positions, carrying the folded films out along with them. Only then could the booms slide out sideways and pull the films across.
keyNumbers: 2 pallets, front and rear
Hold the whole folded shield during launch
Swung down within days of launch
details.madeOf: Composite beams, hinges and latches, plus a set of one-shot release pins and the motors that drive the swing. Covers protected the folded films during launch and were rolled back out of the way.

parts.name: Sunshield pallets

parts.description: Six fast-spinning flywheels inside the bus; speeding one up turns the telescope the other way without firing a thruster.

details.didYouKnow: A worn-out bearing is one of the more common ways for space telescopes to run into trouble, which is why designers carry spare wheels.
details.howItWorks: Spin a heavy wheel faster one way and the spacecraft turns slowly the other way, with no fuel burned at all. With wheels in several directions, the telescope can point anywhere and hold steady. Sunlight pressure on the big shield slowly pushes the wheels' speeds up, so thrusters occasionally fire to unload them.
keyNumbers: Typically 6, so some can fail
Spin at up to thousands of rpm
Unloaded every so often by thrusters
details.madeOf: A precisely balanced steel or titanium rim on very smooth bearings in a sealed housing, driven by a brushless motor with its electronics. They are mounted on isolators so that their hum doesn't reach the mirror.

parts.name: Reaction wheels

summary: A giant infrared space telescope: a 6.5 m mirror of 18 gold-coated hexagons, kept colder than -220 °C behind a tennis-court-sized sunshield of five thin layers, with a spacecraft underneath that points it and talks to Earth.
